kakekotoba.word: 末の松山波こさじとは
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: pledge that waves will never cross it
kakekotoba.interaction: The place name Sue no Matsuyama is invoked literally as a famous locale, but the whole phrase functions as an honkadori-borrowed image whose established meaning ('waves crossing the pine mountain' = the impossible / a broken vow) is activated simultaneously with its literal topographical sense — the mountain is both a real place and the emblem of an unbreakable promise now broken.

jokotoba.function: Sue no Matsuyama functions less as ordinary diction than as an inherited emblematic image (drawn from the Kokinshū anaonymous poem) that stands for the very notion of an unbreakable vow; its invocation here pivots the poem from the private physical image of tear-wringing into the shared cultural shorthand for a vow that should never be broken, deepening the irony that it has been.

honkadori.source_poem: 君をおきてあだし心をわがもたば末の松山波も越えなむ (Anonymous, Kokinshū, Tōhoku-'azuma-uta' section)
honkadori.echoed_phrase: 末の松山波こさじとは / 波も越えなむ
honkadori.function: Motosuke's poem directly echoes the older poem's use of Sue no Matsuyama as a symbol of an impossible event (waves crossing the pine-covered hill) standing for infidelity/breaking a vow. Where the Kokinshū poem asserts confidence that such a betrayal could never happen, Motosuke's poem recalls that very vow now being broken, turning the allusion into a lament over broken faith.

kigo.note: Although 松 (pine) can carry a faint evergreen/winter connotation and 末の松山 is a famous utamakura, in this poem the phrase functions purely as an emblematic place-name for an unbreakable vow rather than as a seasonal image; no natural seasonal marker (blossom, snow, autumn wind, dew, etc.) is present in the poem, so it is best classified as non-seasonal, love-poem imagery (koi no uta) rather than true kigo.

bipartite.kami_theme: The speaker recalls a solemn mutual vow of love, each partner wringing out tear-soaked sleeves as proof of devotion.
bipartite.shimo_theme: The vow was that their bond would be as unbreakable as the legendary impossibility of waves crossing Sue no Matsuyama — an image now recalled with bitter irony, implying the vow has since been broken.
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku establishes the intimate, tearful sincerity of the original promise; the shimo-no-ku reveals the content of that promise through a famous emblematic image of impossibility. The pivot's power lies in the unspoken present-tense irony: quoting the vow verbatim ('did we not pledge...') implies, without stating, that the impossible has in fact happened — the loved one's heart has changed, exposing the earlier tears as futile.
